task.prompt: Differential drive with track width b and wheel speeds vl, vr. Let v be the body forward speed and omega the body yaw rate. For each change below, decide what happens to v and to omega, keeping everything not mentioned fixed (the original omega is not zero). Change (a): the same 0.2 m/s is added to both wheel speeds. Change (b): the track width b is doubled.

fields.label: (a) omega
options: increases by half the added amount

fields.label: (b) v
options: increases by half the added amount

fields.label: (b) omega
options: increases by half the added amount

task.solution: (a) v is the mean of the wheel speeds, so adding 0.2 m/s to both adds 0.2 m/s to v, while omega depends only on the speed difference, which is unchanged. (b) v does not involve b, while omega is a speed difference divided by b, so doubling b halves omega.
hints: v and omega each respond differently to a common offset of both wheels and to the scale of the track width; ask which of them depends on the sum, the difference, and b.
Treat v as built from the sum of the wheel speeds and omega from their difference divided by the track width, then test each change on those.

(a) v is the mean of the wheel speeds, so adding 0.2 m/s to both adds 0.2 m/s to v, while omega depends only on the speed difference, which is unchanged. (b) v does not involve b, while omega is a speed difference divided by b, so doubling b halves omega.
task.remediation: If you said omega changes for (a), you mixed the sum and the difference of the wheel speeds; a common offset moves the body forward without turning it. If you said v halves for (b), you divided the forward speed by b; only the yaw rate depends on b. task.prompt: A robot moves with constant wheel speeds and a non-zero yaw rate omega, so the exact path is a circular arc of radius R around a turn centre. One large time step dt is computed with an Euler rule: the position advances by v dt along the heading the robot had at the START of the step (x += v cos(theta0) dt, y += v sin(theta0) dt) and the heading is updated with theta += omega dt. Compare with the exact arc over the same step. (1) Where does the Euler end position lie relative to the circle of radius R about the turn centre? (2) How does the Euler end heading compare with the exact end heading?

fields.label: Euler end position is
options: On the circle, same point as the exact arc
On the circle, a different point

fields.label: Euler end heading is
fields.answer: Always equal to the exact heading
options: Always equal to the exact heading
Equal to the exact heading only for small omega dt
Smaller than exact by omega dt / 2
Larger than exact by omega dt / 2
Smaller than exact by omega dt

task.solution: (1) Euler moves along the tangent at the start, a straight segment of length v dt, so its end point is at distance sqrt(R^2 + (v dt)^2) > R from the turn centre: outside the circle. (2) The heading update theta += omega dt is already exact for constant omega, so the headings are identical; only the position integration is approximate.
hints: Picture the exact path as a circle and the Euler move as a straight segment that starts on the circle along its tangent line.

A tangent line only touches a circle at its start point; decide whether the other end of a straight segment along it is nearer to or farther from the centre. For the heading, compare the update formula with the exact one.

(1) Euler moves along the tangent at the start, a straight segment of length v dt, so its end point is at distance sqrt(R^2 + (v dt)^2) > R from the turn centre: outside the circle. (2) The heading update theta += omega dt is already exact for constant omega, so the headings are identical; only the position integration is approximate.
task.remediation: A tangent step cannot land on the circle again, so 'on the circle' options mix up Euler with the exact arc; 'inside' would need the segment to cut across the circle (that is a chord, not a tangent). The heading update is the same as the exact one, so any heading difference option misreads which part is approximate. task.prompt: Heading is stored wrapped into (-pi, pi]. (1) Does replacing a heading by its wrapped value change the position computed from it through sin and cos of the heading? It changes the position only when the wheel speeds are unequal

task.prompt: You pass your edited lab self-check for an ideal differential-drive integrator (exact arc, no slip, ideal encoders). Consider these claims. (a) On the cases the self-check ran, the functions returned values within the kit's tolerances. (b) The functions are correct for every possible input. More self-check fixtures generated from the same ideal model and tolerances
A smaller integration step and higher-precision arithmetic, tested on simulated data
A second independent implementation of the same ideal equations, cross-checked in simulation
Repeating the self-check on a faster computer

task.solution: Only (a) is what a passing self-check shows. task.prompt: Convention: differential drive; track width b is the distance between the wheel contact points; vl (left) and vr (right) are LINEAR wheel speeds in m/s; heading is relative to world +x, counter-clockwise positive, in radians; constant speeds, no slip. task.solution: v = (vl + vr)/2 = (0.62 + 0.29)/2 = 0.455 m/s. omega = (vr - vl)/b = (0.29 - 0.62)/0.44 = -0.75 rad/s (full track width b, right minus left).
hints: v describes the axle midpoint, and omega describes how the speed difference between the wheels turns the body about the vertical axis; check which wheel is faster and which way that turns the robot.
Average the two wheel speeds for v. For omega take right minus left and divide by the full track width b = 0.44 m, keeping the sign.
v = (vl + vr)/2 = (0.62 + 0.29)/2 = 0.455 m/s. omega = (vr - vl)/b = (0.29 - 0.62)/0.44 = -0.75 rad/s (full track width b, right minus left).
task.remediation: If omega has the opposite sign (0.75) you subtracted in the wrong order or swapped the wheels; dividing by b/2 instead of the full b doubles it to -1.5. task.prompt: Convention: differential drive; track width b is the distance between the wheel contact points; vl (left) and vr (right) are LINEAR wheel speeds in m/s; heading is relative to world +x, counter-clockwise positive, in radians; constant speeds, no slip. task.solution: The zero-heading displacement is expressed in the robot's start frame, so it is rotated by theta0 (the orientation of that frame) and added to the start position. task.prompt: Convention: differential drive; track width b is the distance between the wheel contact points; vl (left) and vr (right) are LINEAR wheel speeds in m/s; heading is relative to world +x, counter-clockwise positive, in radians; constant speeds, no slip. A robot has track width b = 0.64 m, left wheel speed vl = 0.17 m/s and right wheel speed vr = 0.65 m/s. Give the body forward speed v (m/s) and the signed yaw rate omega (rad/s, counter-clockwise positive). Give 3 decimal places; tolerance ±0.001.
task.solution: v = (vl + vr)/2 = (0.17 + 0.65)/2 = 0.41 m/s. omega = (vr - vl)/b = (0.65 - 0.17)/0.64 = 0.75 rad/s (full track width b, right minus left).
hints: v describes the axle midpoint, and omega describes how the speed difference between the wheels turns the body about the vertical axis; check which wheel is faster and which way that turns the robot.
Average the two wheel speeds for v. For omega take right minus left and divide by the full track width b = 0.64 m, keeping the sign.
v = (vl + vr)/2 = (0.17 + 0.65)/2 = 0.41 m/s. omega = (vr - vl)/b = (0.65 - 0.17)/0.64 = 0.75 rad/s (full track width b, right minus left).
task.remediation: If omega has the opposite sign (-0.75) you subtracted in the wrong order or swapped the wheels; dividing by b/2 instead of the full b doubles it to 1.5. A positive omega means the right wheel is faster (counter-clockwise turn). task.prompt: Convention: differential drive; track width b is the distance between the wheel contact points; vl (left) and vr (right) are LINEAR wheel speeds in m/s; heading is relative to world +x, counter-clockwise positive, in radians; constant speeds, no slip. The pose (x, y, heading) in the world frame is (-1.4 m, 0.7 m, -0.6 rad). The wheels hold vl = 0.5 m/s and vr = 0.2 m/s for dt = 2.5 s with track width b = 0.5 m. Integrate the motion exactly along its circular arc (not with Euler steps) and give the final world x, y and heading (any equivalent angle modulo 2 pi is accepted). Give 3 decimal places; tolerance ±0.001.
task.solution: v = 0.35 m/s, omega = -0.6 rad/s, turn angle phi = omega dt = -1.5 rad, R = v/omega = -0.5833 m. x = x0 + R(sin(theta0 + phi) - sin(theta0)) = -1.2258; y = y0 - R(cos(theta0 + phi) - cos(theta0)) = -0.0759; heading = theta0 + phi = -2.1 rad.
hints: Reduce the wheel speeds to a forward speed and a yaw rate first. The robot then follows a circle whose position formulas must be measured from its initial heading, not from the x axis.

Compute v, omega, phi = omega dt and the radius R = v/omega. Then the world displacement uses the difference between the sine (and cosine) of the end heading and of the start heading -0.6 rad, scaled by R; add it to the start position.

v = 0.35 m/s, omega = -0.6 rad/s, turn angle phi = omega dt = -1.5 rad, R = v/omega = -0.5833 m. x = x0 + R(sin(theta0 + phi) - sin(theta0)) = -1.2258; y = y0 - R(cos(theta0 + phi) - cos(theta0)) = -0.0759; heading = theta0 + phi = -2.1 rad.
task.remediation: Common slips on this item: Euler (straight along the start heading) gives x = -0.6778, y = 0.2059; a midpoint step of length v dt gives x = -1.2084, y = -0.1538; forgetting to rotate the arc by the initial heading gives x = -0.8181, y = 0.1579; omega with b/2 gives x = -1.6938, y = 0.1977, heading = -3.6; swapped wheels give heading = 0.9; a calculator in degree mode gives x = -1.3847, y = 0.6996. If your answer matches one, the slip is in that step, not in the arithmetic. task.prompt: Convention: differential drive; track width b is the distance between the wheel contact points; vl (left) and vr (right) are LINEAR wheel speeds in m/s; heading is relative to world +x, counter-clockwise positive, in radians; constant speeds, no slip. task.solution: Segment 1: v = 0.35, omega = -0.75, ends at (0.8767, -0.8684) with heading 0.7 rad. Segment 2 must start from that pose: v = 0.25, omega = 0.75, giving (0.7254, -0.2863) and heading 2.95 rad.

Integrate segment 1 exactly from the start pose, keep its end position and end heading, and use that pose as the start of the exact arc for segment 2.
Segment 1: v = 0.35, omega = -0.75, ends at (0.8767, -0.8684) with heading 0.7 rad. Segment 2 must start from that pose: v = 0.25, omega = 0.75, giving (0.7254, -0.2863) and heading 2.95 rad.
